instruction: Compare the original and rewrite directly. Independently identify substantive reasoning relations in the original and check all against the rewrite, including omissions, additions, conditions, timing, actors, causal direction, and scope. Return status preserved only when all substantive reasoning survives. Use changed for a material change and uncertain for unresolved meaning. Give concrete evidence for your assessment. Wording and presentation order may differ.

documents.original:
A familiar brand can reuse a box design across several piece counts. Label each donated puzzle with its title and stated count from the manufacturer's panel so people can compare likely commitments. A thousand-piece puzzle with distinct illustrated characters feels different from a thousand pieces of sky. Let contributors add a plain description of the image and the stretches that made their build challenging. People vary in how much a missing piece bothers them. Keep playable incomplete puzzles together and show the known gap on the box image with a removable note so takers can decide. An already assembled jigsaw is easier to take down when large sections are turned over first. Invite the last builder to check the backs and separate connected pieces before donating it for a fresh solve.

People with limited grip may find small, thickly packed pieces awkward to handle. Mark large-piece sets by their actual piece size and keep a sample outline on their cards for comparison. A small child may reach whatever is on the bottom shelf while a caregiver browses. Reserve that space for boxed children's puzzles and keep the original age guidance visible on each one. An image printed on the lid may be the only reference available while assembling. Check that the picture is legible and include a clean image from the donor when a damaged lid needs a substitute. Damp cardboard can spoil the boxes beside it once a cupboard closes. Examine incoming boxes in good light and ask the donor to take back any that show moisture or mildew.

People may forget a puzzle's title by the time they discover a problem at home. Give accepted boxes a short identifier so a resident can report an issue without trying to describe the artwork. When a reported missing piece turns up under the dining table, a whole puzzle can become complete again. Keep found pieces in labeled envelopes behind the desk and match them using the puzzle identifier. Volunteers need a way to tell high turnover from slow accumulation. Tally incoming and outgoing boxes during each opening and use the trend to decide when the next donation window can fit. Neighbors sometimes need to picture a completed puzzle before they choose it. Invite builders to contribute a snapshot for a noticeboard and put its box identifier underneath so someone can look for the same one.
documents.rewrite:
A familiar brand may use the same box design for several piece counts. For each donated puzzle, copy the title and stated piece count from the manufacturer's panel onto a label so people can compare how much work the puzzles are likely to take. Assembling a thousand pieces depicting distinct illustrated characters feels different from assembling a thousand pieces of sky. Let contributors describe the image in plain language and point out the parts they found challenging to put together. A missing piece bothers some people more than others. Group playable incomplete puzzles together and mark the known gap on the box image with a removable note so takers can decide for themselves. Turning large sections over first makes an assembled jigsaw easier to take apart. Invite the last builder to check the backs and separate connected pieces before donating the puzzle for someone to solve afresh.

Small, tightly packed pieces can be awkward to handle for people with limited grip. Label large-piece sets with the actual piece size and keep a sample outline on each card for comparison. While a caregiver browses, a small child may reach whatever is on the bottom shelf. Set that shelf aside for boxed children's puzzles and keep the original age guidance visible on each box. The picture on the lid may be the only reference a builder has. Check that the image is legible. If a damaged lid calls for a substitute, include a clean image from the donor. Once the cupboard is closed, damp cardboard can spoil neighboring boxes. Inspect incoming boxes in good light and ask donors to take back any that show signs of moisture or mildew.

By the time people discover a problem at home, they may have forgotten the puzzle's title. Give each accepted box a short identifier so a resident can report a problem without having to describe the artwork. A puzzle can be complete again when a piece reported missing turns up under the dining table. Keep found pieces in labeled envelopes behind the desk and use the puzzle identifier to match them. Volunteers need to distinguish high turnover from a collection that is slowly growing. At each opening, tally the boxes coming in and going out. Use the trend to decide when there's room for the next donation window. Sometimes neighbors need to picture a finished puzzle before choosing it. Invite builders to contribute a snapshot for the noticeboard, and write the box identifier beneath the photo so someone can look for that puzzle.
